A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study despite the changed title. The shared tasks, representation analysis, and retained GPT results can be matched reliably. All 11 pages of v1 and 12 pages of v2, including appendices, were readable.

before.justification: v1 reports original neuron-difference analyses, behavior-classification experiments, and targeted versus random intervention results in Figures 3–6 and Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v2 retains original GPT results and adds LLaMA experiments, base-versus-adapter analysis, and retraining and cross-task transfer results in Figures 3, 5–6 and Tables 2–4.

M1.justification: v2 adds a frozen-base LoRA fine-tuning path and corresponding activation extraction for LLaMA 3.2 to the GPT-based workflow. The central procedure remains paired representation extraction, NMD calculation, Pearson-correlation neuron selection, per-layer classification, and activation shifting.

E1.justification: Both versions use adapted bAbI induction-style in-context inference and synthetic addition of four integers from 1–999, with injected memorization associations. The new transfer experiments reuse these tasks; different models and intervention sources change experimental settings rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The random comparator is removed from the retained GPT comparisons: v1 Tables 1–2 contain random-control rows, whereas v2 Table 1 does not. v2 introduces random controls in the new transfer experiments, but changes their construction from redistributing the original intervention shifts to sampling shifts uniformly from a bounded interval. This substantially revises the paper's sole control strategy.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation using pretrained LLaMA 3.2-3B with frozen base weights and LoRA adapters. It also introduces separate base/adapter query-and-value measurements, intervention transfer to independently retrained adapters, and intervention transfer between tasks. These are substantial new experimental protocols; the additional descriptions of existing data generation do not establish that the GPT experiments changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained layer-wise and classifier-training-size analyses, v2 adds three substantive investigations: attribution of NMD to the pretrained base versus LoRA adapters, robustness across adapter retraining, and cross-task transferability. Section 5, Figure 6, and Tables 3–4 directly test questions left for future work in v1.

E5.justification: v2 Section 5.2 newly reports retraining adapters with a different random seed while holding data and hyperparameters fixed. This adds seed-variation information and an experiment, rather than an aggregate uncertainty estimate. Neither version explains the existing shaded classifier bands or reports significance tests or defined confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The GPT intervention percentages are retained unchanged, and the GPT classifier plots are reused. v2 adds LLaMA results and retraining/transfer outcomes. Table 4 reports 65.9%/22.8% steering success when arithmetic-derived neurons are applied to in-context inference, versus 15.4%/9.3% for the reverse transfer. The original GPT random-control entries and reported rephrasing-induced behavior-change frequencies are removed.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theorems or proofs, and the NMD definition remains equivalent. The explicit signed, NMD-scaled activation-update equation added to the v2 appendix formalizes the existing intervention description without introducing a new derivation or formal property.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes identifying, predicting, and steering behavior in experimental-scale models. v2 makes validation on a pretrained model and stability across retraining and tasks central contributions, claiming robust, reusable neuron mappings and separable neural pathways. Behavior prediction remains in the paper but is no longer a principal research question.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting behavior signals to the pretrained base and asymmetric transfer to task-specific neuron specialization. It distinguishes steering success from correctness and adds limitations concerning the restricted definition of generalization and the linear intervention mechanism. v1's explanation linking final-layer NMD differences to output format is removed.

D1.justification: The v2 appendix adds data-generation vocabularies and sampling probabilities, LoRA rank/alpha/dropout/target modules, representation-pair counts, and an explicit intervention equation. It removes v1's selected topN=0.1 and intervention alpha=1 or 5. The new pair-count list also reverses the GPT-2/GPT-2-medium task assignments relative to the model-description text, introducing a reproducibility inconsistency.

R1.justification: v2 substantially replaces the neuron-localization and behavior-identification survey with discussion of memorization disentanglement and activation steering. New references include Huang et al. (2024), Schwarzschild et al. (2024), Chen et al. (2024a), Panickssery et al. (2023), and Suri et al. (2025). References such as Meng et al. (2022), Stolfo et al. (2023), and several brain-alignment works disappear, shifting the research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, dataset explanations, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. The standalone Behavior Identification section is folded into Section 3.3, intervention material gains subsections, and generalizability becomes a main section. Limitations move after the conclusion, the appendix is reorganized, and the title and author list change.

P2.justification: v1's motivational Figure 1 is removed, while its method diagram survives as v2 Figure 1. Existing GPT heatmaps and classifier plots are combined into panels; LLaMA and base/adapter figures are added. The original task-specific tables are reorganized into model-specific tables, with two additional transfer tables. These substantially change the visual organization.

improvement.justification: The pretrained-LLaMA validation and retraining/transfer experiments address important untested extensions acknowledged in v1, and the appendix provides useful implementation details. These gains are limited by removal of the original matched-shift random comparisons and selected intervention hyperparameters, plus stronger modularity claims despite weak reverse-transfer results in Table 4. The paper gains empirical support, but its controls and reproducibility do not improve consistently.
